project.title: FunnelLens: Data Analyst Case Study on a Messy E-commerce Funnel
project.tagline: Take one messy e-commerce export from raw CSVs to a tested, reproducible recommendation the Head of Product can act on, with a data contract, statistics that adjust for confounders, CI, a dashboard and an AI narrator that cannot invent numbers
project.description: Mobile is about 69 % of FunnelLens's sessions but only about 61 % of its revenue, and the Head of Product wants a quarter of engineering time to rebuild the mobile checkout. Over nine phases you find out what the data supports, like a professional analytics team: turn the request into answerable questions with acceptance criteria, write a data contract and an analysis plan with ADRs, then build the analysis test-first in your track: load four deliberately messy CSVs as text, apply documented cleaning rules that count every row they drop, check the contract, build the funnel by device, channel and week, and test the hypothesis three ways (a two-proportion z test, a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test that adjusts for acquisition channel and exposes a Simpson's paradox, and Welch's t test on order values) before sizing the opportunity against the rebuild threshold. Golden answers, invariants and contract-violation tests pin every number, and the Python, SQL and R tracks must agree to 1e-9. CI executes the notebook or R Markdown report and checks parity; a Streamlit dashboard with an optional AI narrator (numbered facts in, guardrails out, a deterministic template as fallback) ships in Docker. Then a data refresh breaks the pipeline on purpose: a new acquisition channel and a broken tracking week lead to a contract version bump, monitoring, a post-mortem and v1.1. Pick Python (pandas, Jupyter), SQL (DuckDB) or R (tidyverse, R Markdown); the data, contract, golden answers and dashboard are shared. Everything runs on a laptop with no paid service and no API key.

prerequisites.title: Git and the command line basics
One of: Python with pandas, SQL (SELECT, GROUP BY, JOIN, window functions) or R with dplyr
Descriptive statistics: proportions, means, confidence intervals, p-values

outcomes: Turn a stakeholder's solution ("rebuild the mobile checkout") into answerable questions, decision thresholds and acceptance criteria
Write a data contract (schema, accepted values, checks with severities) and an analysis plan with ADRs before touching the data
Load messy exports defensively and clean them with documented rules that count every row they change, without silently multiplying revenue in a join
Build a conversion funnel by device, channel and week and spot a Simpson's paradox before it misleads a decision
Test a hypothesis three ways (two-proportion z, Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel adjusted for a confounder, Welch's t) and size the opportunity against a business threshold
Pin an analysis with golden answers, invariants and contract-violation tests, and make three implementations agree to 1e-9
Make a notebook or R Markdown report reproducible from a clean checkout, and execute it in CI with GitHub Actions
Ship a Streamlit dashboard in Docker with an AI narrator that only sees aggregates, is checked by guardrails and falls back to a deterministic template
Handle a breaking data refresh: version the contract, add monitoring, exclude a broken week on purpose and write a blameless post-mortem
Use AI assistants deliberately and verify every number they produce
project.ai_feature: An optional AI insight narrator on the dashboard: it receives only numbered aggregate facts from answers.json (never rows or ids) and writes a short summary for the Head of Product. Guardrails reject any answer with an unknown citation, a number that is not a correct rounding of a fact, an unlisted date, causal language or a missing caveat, and the dashboard then shows a deterministic template instead. Offline by default; any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (a local Ollama, or a free Gemini/Groq key) can be plugged in
project.portfolio_blurb: Built FunnelLens, an end-to-end data analyst case study on a deliberately messy e-commerce export (sessions, events, orders, users): a versioned data contract with severity-graded checks, documented cleaning rules that count every dropped row, a funnel by device, channel and week, and three hypothesis tests (two-proportion z, Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel adjusted for acquisition channel, which exposed a Simpson's paradox, and Welch's t). The evidence did not support the proposed mobile checkout rebuild (adjusted payment odds ratio 0.71, 95 % CI 0.62 to 0.81, but an uplift of about ₹16 lakh a month against a ₹25 lakh threshold), so I recommended a targeted experiment. Golden answers, invariants and contract-violation tests; Python, SQL and R implementations that agree to 1e-9; a reproducible notebook/R Markdown report executed in GitHub Actions CI; a Streamlit dashboard in Docker with a guard-railed AI narrator; and, after a data refresh broke the pipeline, a contract version bump, weekly monitoring and a blameless post-mortem (v1.1).

phases.title: Setup and the brief
phases.heading: Phase 0 · Setup and the brief
phases.why_md:
An analysis nobody else can re-run is an opinion with charts. Professional analysts start where
engineers start: a repository that installs with one command, data whose origin you can prove, tests
that say what "right" means, and a log of how AI helped. In this phase you set up the tools for
**one** track, read the brief and the data, run the starter, meet the pending tests and the contract
that will guide you, open your first pull request and start your `AI_LOG.md`. You will not compute a
single number yet, on purpose: first you learn what question is being asked and what the data can say.
objectives: Fork the repository **with all branches and tags**, clone it and add the `upstream` remote.
Pick a track (Python, SQL or R), install its toolchain on Windows (WSL2), macOS or Linux, and run `make lint test`.
Explain the brief in two sentences: who decides what, and why "rebuild the mobile checkout" is a solution, not a question.
Prove the export in `data/raw/2026-06` is exactly the published one (`generate_data.py --check`) and list three defects you can see in the raw CSVs.
Open a pull request that passes CI and write your first `AI_LOG.md` entry.

steps.title: Fork and clone (keep the tags!)
steps.content_md:
1. On GitHub open `AICanCode-org/analyst-case-study` → **Fork**. **Untick "Copy the `main` branch
   only"**. The `solution` branch and the `phase-N-end` tags are your safety net in later phases.
2. Clone **your** fork and connect the original as `upstream`:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<you>/analyst-case-study.git
   cd analyst-case-study
   git remote add upstream https://github.com/AICanCode-org/analyst-case-study.git
   git fetch upstream --tags
   git tag -l 'phase-*'      # phase-0-end … phase-8-end
   ```
3. **Windows:** do all of this inside **WSL2** (Ubuntu) and keep the repo in the Linux file system
   (`~/code/analyst-case-study`), not under `/mnt/c`.

steps.title: Install the tools for ONE track
steps.content_md:
Every track needs Git, `make` and Python 3.11+ (the data generator, the parity script and the
dashboard are Python). Run the doctor script; it tells you exactly what is missing:
```bash
scripts/doctor.sh
```

<!-- track:python -->
**Python track:** pandas, Jupyter, SciPy and statsmodels, installed into a virtual environment.
```bash
cd tracks/python && make install     # creates .venv with the pinned versions
.venv/bin/python -c "import pandas, scipy, statsmodels; print(pandas.__version__)"
```
Open the notebook with `.venv/bin/jupyter lab notebooks/analysis.ipynb` (or VS Code with the
Jupyter extension, selecting `.venv` as the kernel).
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL track:** DuckDB, an in-process analytical database: no server, it reads the CSVs directly.
The analysis is written in `sql/*.sql`; a thin Python runner sets variables and writes `answers.json`.
```bash
cd tracks/sql && make install        # .venv with duckdb, sqlfluff, pytest
.venv/bin/python -c "import duckdb; print(duckdb.sql(\"SELECT count(*) FROM '../../data/raw/2026-06/orders.csv'\"))"
```
Optional: the DuckDB CLI (`brew install duckdb`, or the binary from duckdb.org) to explore by hand.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:r -->
**R track:** R 4.3+ with the tidyverse core, testthat, lintr and R Markdown (pandoc renders it).
```bash
sudo apt install r-base pandoc        # Ubuntu/WSL; macOS/Windows: R from CRAN + RStudio (includes pandoc)
cd tracks/r && make install            # installs the packages listed in DESCRIPTION (pak)
Rscript -e 'packageVersion("dplyr")'
```
RStudio users: open `tracks/r` as a project; the package is loaded with `devtools::load_all()` or
`pkgload::load_all()`.
<!-- /track -->

steps.title: Read the brief and the data
steps.content_md:
1. Read the top of `README.md` (the situation) and `contract/questions.md` §1 (the decision and the
   eight questions). Write down, in your own words: **who decides, what, and what a wrong decision costs.**
2. Read `data/README.md`, then look at the raw files themselves. They are small on purpose:
   ```bash
   head -5 data/raw/2026-06/sessions.csv
   grep -c '/' data/raw/2026-06/sessions.csv          # rows with the day-first date format
   cut -d, -f4 data/raw/2026-06/users.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -12   # city spellings
   python3 scripts/generate_data.py --check            # byte-identical to the seeded generator
   ```
3. Note three defects you can see without any code (duplicate rows? two date formats? amounts as
   text?). Phase 2 turns each of them into a rule.

steps.title: Run the checks and meet the pending tests and the contract
steps.content_md:
```bash
make lint test
```
All the tests are **skipped**. They are *pending*: the complete test suite is already written and
switched off in one list per track:

| Track | Pending list |
|---|---|
| Python | `tracks/python/tests/conftest.py` (`PENDING`) |
| SQL | `tracks/sql/tests/conftest.py` (`PENDING`) |
| R | `tracks/r/tests/testthat/helper-funnellens.R` (`PENDING`) |

Each entry names a milestone ("Phase 3 M1 - cleaning rules and the issue counts"). In Phase 3 you
delete one entry at a time, watch the tests go red, and make them green.

Now open the four files of `contract/` that make "right" precise:
- `questions.md`: every cleaning rule, in order, and every formula;
- `data-contract.yaml`: the columns each CSV must have and the checks (an `error` stops the run);
- `answers.schema.json`: the shape of `answers.json`, the one output every track writes;
- `fixtures/tiny/` + `tiny-expected.json`: a 14-session export small enough to check by hand, and
  `golden/answers-2026-06.json`: the reference answers for the real export.

steps.title: Your first pull request
steps.content_md:
1. Create a branch: `git switch -c chore/phase-0-setup`.
2. Fill in the first entry in `AI_LOG.md`, e.g. how an assistant explained a `duckdb` / `pandas` /
   `readr` error during the install and how you checked its advice.
3. Commit and push, then open a PR **in your fork** against your `main`:
   ```bash
   git add AI_LOG.md
   git commit -m "docs: start AI_LOG for phase 0"
   git push -u origin chore/phase-0-setup
   ```
4. Open the **Actions** tab. Forks have Actions switched off until you click **"I understand my
   workflows, go ahead and enable them"**. CI runs lint + unit tests for all three tracks. Wait for
   green, fill in the PR template and merge.

I'm on <Windows 11 + WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 | macOS 15 | Ubuntu 24.04>. I want to run a <Python 3.12 with
pandas and Jupyter | DuckDB 1.x from Python | R 4.5 with the tidyverse, testthat and R Markdown>
project. Here is the output of scripts/doctor.sh: <paste output>. Give me the exact commands to
install what is missing, explain each one in one line, and tell me how to verify each install.

ai_prompts.title: Restate the brief as a decision
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is a stakeholder brief: <paste the "situation" paragraph of README.md and contract/questions.md §1>.
Restate it as: (1) the decision to be made, by whom, (2) the cost of each wrong decision, (3) the
question the data must answer, (4) three alternative explanations for "69 % of sessions but 61 % of
revenue" that would NOT call for a checkout rebuild. Do not compute anything and do not guess numbers.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking every claim against the brief (assistants add details that are not there, such as a conversion rate or a budget), and keeping at least one alternative explanation that involves *who* uses mobile (traffic mix) rather than *how* the checkout works. You will test them in Phase 3.

ai_prompts.title: Read a raw file like an analyst
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here are the header and 15 sample rows of a raw CSV export: <paste head -16 data/raw/2026-06/orders.csv>.
List every data-quality problem you can see or suspect, how you would detect each one in code, and
what you would ask the data owner. Do not clean anything yet.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: finding each problem in the real file with `grep` or a quick count (an assistant may "see" problems that are not in your sample), and comparing your list with `contract/questions.md` §2. These rows are synthetic; with real customer data you would paste column names and aggregates only, never rows.

quiz.q: Why must you untick "Copy the main branch only" when forking?
options: Otherwise GitHub Actions is disabled in the fork
Otherwise the `solution` branch and phase tags are missing from your fork
Otherwise you cannot open pull requests
Otherwise the CSV files are not copied
quiz.explanation: Forks copy only `main` by default. The tags (`phase-N-end`) live on the `solution` branch; without them you cannot compare your work or catch up. Fix it later with `git fetch upstream --tags`.

quiz.q: The Head of Product says "rebuild the mobile checkout". What is your job?
options: Prove the Head of Product right, since they own the decision
Prove them wrong, to show independence
Find out what the data supports and say it clearly enough that the decision can be made, including what you could not establish
Build the rebuild's business case
quiz.explanation: A stakeholder's proposed solution is a hypothesis. The analysis is judged on whether the conclusion follows from the evidence and states its limits, not on agreement.

quiz.q: Why are the raw CSV files read as text, and never "fixed" by hand?
options: Text is faster to read
The CSV format cannot store numbers
Type guessing hides defects (a `₹1,299` becomes missing silently), and a hand edit cannot be reproduced or counted; the cleaning rules do it in code and count every row
GitHub cannot store edited CSV files
quiz.explanation: Defensive loading means you decide every type yourself, so every rejected value is visible and counted in `data_quality.issues`. `generate_data.py --check` proves nobody touched the raw files.

quiz.q: Why are all tests skipped in the starter?
options: They are flaky
CI is too slow to run them
They describe behaviour you build in Phases 3-4 and are switched on one milestone at a time
They only run on the solution branch
quiz.explanation: The full suite is written up-front (test-first). Deleting a line from the pending list turns a group back on, so you always have a clear red → green target.

quiz.q: What is `contract/fixtures/tiny/` for?
options: A smaller export to save disk space
A 14-session export small enough to check by hand, with every expected count and rate written down, so unit tests can pin each rule exactly
Training data for the AI narrator
The data of a different shop
quiz.explanation: Real exports are too big to check by eye. The tiny fixture contains one example of each defect; `tiny-expected.json` says what every rule must produce on it, so a wrong rule fails a test in milliseconds.

quiz.q: Which of these may you paste into an AI prompt for this project?
options: Your `.env` file with an LLM API key
500 rows of a real customer orders export
Column names, your own code, an error message and aggregate numbers
Another student's notebook
quiz.explanation: Secrets and row-level personal data never go into prompts. The FunnelLens data is synthetic, but practise the habit you will need at work: aggregates and code, not rows.

phases.title: Requirements: questions, decisions and acceptance criteria
phases.heading: Phase 1 · Requirements: questions, decisions and acceptance criteria
phases.why_md:
Most analyses fail before the first line of code: they answer a question nobody asked, or they never
say what result would change the decision. "Rebuild the mobile checkout" is a stakeholder's
*solution*. Your first job is to turn it into questions the data can answer, a **decision rule agreed
before anyone looks at the numbers**, and acceptance criteria a reviewer can check. Writing the rule
first is what stops an analysis from being bent, consciously or not, towards the answer someone
wants (the "garden of forking paths"). The result is `spec/requirements.md`, one page a Head of
Product, an engineering lead and a finance partner can all sign.
objectives: Map the stakeholders of a decision, what each needs and what each would like the answer to be.
Turn a proposed solution into 5-8 measurable questions, each linked to a metric and a `contract/questions.md` section.
Write a decision rule with a significance level and a minimum business effect (₹ per month) before seeing the data, and justify both numbers.
State what an observational, sampled export can and cannot establish.
Write testable acceptance criteria and a risk list for an analysis, and file the questions as GitHub issues.

steps.title: Map the stakeholders
steps.content_md:
Copy the headings of `spec/requirements.md` (they are already there with `TODO`s). For at least four
stakeholders (Head of Product, mobile engineering lead, finance, marketing), write one line each:
*what they need from you* and *what they hope you will find*. Notice the conflicts: the Head of
Product hopes the checkout is the problem; marketing would rather it was not the traffic it buys.
Naming these hopes up-front is how you stay independent of them.

steps.title: From "rebuild it" to questions
steps.content_md:
Ask *why* until you reach something measurable. "Mobile revenue is flat" → "is mobile's revenue
share lower than its session share?" → "at which funnel step does mobile lose people?" → "is that step
worse for mobile users who arrived the same way as desktop users?". For each question, write the
metric and its exact definition. The eight questions of `contract/questions.md` §1 are the agreed set
for this course; your job is to understand why each is there and what decision depends on it. Add
one question of your own to "Out of scope" if it cannot be answered with this export.

steps.title: The decision rule, before the data
steps.content_md:
Write down, *now*, which result leads to which recommendation:
1. If the payment-step gap is **not** significant after adjusting for acquisition channel
   (α = 0.05): **do not rebuild** (`no_checkout_gap_found`).
2. If it is significant and closing it would be worth **at least ₹25 lakh a month**: **rebuild**.
3. If it is significant but worth less: **run a targeted experiment** on the payment step first.

Justify the numbers in one line each: α = 0.05 is the team's convention for a one-off decision; a
rebuild costs about a quarter of a squad (≈ ₹75 lakh fully loaded) and must pay back within three
months, hence ₹25 lakh a month. Both are in `contract/data-contract.yaml` (`analysis:`) so code and
memo use the same numbers. Changing them after seeing the results needs a written reason.

steps.title: What the data can and cannot say
steps.content_md:
Write §5 of the requirements: six months, a 1-in-20 sample of sessions (so counts must be scaled by
20 for business figures), one country, and **observational**: users chose their device and channel,
nobody randomised them. That means an association, however significant, is not proof that the
checkout *causes* the gap. Say so now; the memo will repeat it.

steps.title: Acceptance criteria and risks
steps.content_md:
Write at least eight acceptance criteria a reviewer can check without trusting you, for example:
"`make report` runs top to bottom from a clean checkout", "every cleaning rule reports how many rows
it changed", "a failing `error` check stops the run with exit code 3 before any number is written",
"the three tracks produce identical `answers.json` (1e-9)", "every effect is reported with a 95 %
interval", "the memo states the recommendation and the observational caveat". Then at least five
risks with the mitigation: confounding by channel, Simpson's paradox, a join that multiplies
revenue, peeking at many cuts until one is significant, a tracking break, an AI summary that
invents a number.

steps.title: One issue per question
steps.content_md:
Create one GitHub issue per question with the **Analysis question** template ("As a Head of
Product, I want to know whether mobile pays less after checkout, within the same channel, so that I
can decide on the rebuild"), with acceptance criteria and an estimate. Link the issues from the
requirements file. Commit on a branch, open a PR, merge when CI is green.

ai_prompts.title: Play the stakeholder
ai_prompts.prompt:
You are the Head of Product of a mid-sized Indian e-commerce company. Mobile is ~69 % of sessions but
~61 % of revenue, and you are convinced the mobile checkout is broken. I am your new analyst. Answer my
questions in character, in 2-3 sentences each, and push back when I try to delay. Stay consistent:
do not invent data I could check. My first question: what decision will you take, and by when?
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: writing down the decision, deadline and constraints it gave you and checking they are consistent with the brief; anything new (a deadline, a budget) is role-play, not a fact, and must be confirmed with the real stakeholder (here: the brief and `data-contract.yaml`).

ai_prompts.title: Make my questions measurable
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here are my draft analysis questions and the data dictionary: <paste your questions and data/README.md>.
For each question: (1) the metric that answers it, with numerator, denominator and unit of analysis,
(2) whether this export can answer it, (3) the confounder that could fake the result. Flag any
question that is really a solution in disguise.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking each metric against `contract/questions.md` (same numerator and denominator?) and rejecting any metric that needs data the export does not have (for example page-load times or app versions).

ai_prompts.title: Attack my decision rule
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is my decision rule for a checkout-rebuild decision: <paste §4 of your requirements>. Act as a
sceptical finance partner and a sceptical statistician. List the ways this rule could lead to a
wrong decision (thresholds, multiple comparisons, sampling, observational data) and what I should add.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: keeping only objections you can explain in your own words, and checking that each one is either handled by the plan (channel adjustment, a single pre-registered test, a threshold in rupees) or written down as a risk. Do not let it talk you into changing the thresholds without a business reason.

deliverables.text: `spec/requirements.md` without `TODO`s: decision, stakeholders, questions, decision rule, data limits, acceptance criteria, risks, out of scope.
The decision rule states α, the ₹ threshold and where each number comes from.
At least eight testable acceptance criteria and five risks with mitigations.
One GitHub issue per question, linked from the requirements.
An `AI_LOG.md` entry for at least one prompt, with what you rejected.

quiz.q: Why write the decision rule before computing anything?
options: It makes the analysis faster
So the result cannot bend the rule: thresholds chosen after seeing the numbers invite picking the ones that give the hoped-for answer
Because the rule is needed to load the data
Because GitHub requires it
quiz.explanation: Pre-registering the rule (and the test) is the analyst's defence against the garden of forking paths: with enough cuts and thresholds, any dataset "supports" any decision.

quiz.q: Where does the ₹25 lakh a month threshold come from?
options: It is the industry standard for checkouts
It is the largest uplift in the data
From the cost of the rebuild (≈ ₹75 lakh of engineering) and the agreed three-month payback
From the p-value

quiz.q: The export is a 1-in-20 sample of sessions. What does that change?
options: Nothing: rates are the same
Rates and tests are fine on the sample, but counts and rupee figures must be scaled by 20 to describe the business
The p-values must be multiplied by 20
The sample cannot be used for statistics
quiz.explanation: Proportions estimated from a random sample are unbiased; totals are not. The opportunity sizing (Q7) divides by `sample_rate`.

quiz.q: Why is "mobile has a lower purchase rate after checkout" not proof that the checkout causes it?
options: Because the sample is too small
Because the data is observational: mobile and desktop users differ (for example in how they arrived), and such differences can produce the gap
Because purchase is not an event in the data
Because p-values cannot be computed on proportions
quiz.explanation: Nobody randomised users to devices. Adjusting for a known confounder (channel) helps; only an experiment can show cause. That is why "run a targeted experiment" is one of the outcomes.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good acceptance criterion for an analysis?
options: "The analysis is high quality"
"The charts look professional"
"`make report` runs top to bottom from a clean checkout and the three tracks' answers.json are identical"
"The Head of Product agrees with the result"
quiz.explanation: An acceptance criterion is something a reviewer can check without trusting you. Agreement is not a criterion; reproducibility and parity are.

quiz.q: Which risk does comparing mobile and desktop *within each acquisition channel* address?
options: A join that multiplies revenue
A tracking break in one week
Confounding by traffic mix: if mobile gets more of a low-converting channel, the overall gap can be a mix effect
An AI summary inventing numbers
quiz.explanation: Stratifying by channel compares like with like. It is the core of Q4 (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel) and the check for a Simpson's paradox.

A decision rule written before the data protects the analysis from forking paths.
Business thresholds come from the business case and live in the contract.
What an observational, sampled export can and cannot establish.
Acceptance criteria and risks a reviewer can check, filed as issues.

phases.title: Design: data contract, analysis plan and ADRs
phases.heading: Phase 2 · Design: data contract, analysis plan and ADRs
phases.why_md:
In software, design is the architecture. In analysis, design is **deciding how the question will be
answered before the data can influence you**: which rows count, which test, which confounder, what
the output looks like and when the pipeline must refuse to produce a number. FunnelLens writes this
down in two places: a *data contract* (the rules a machine checks) and an *analysis plan* (the
reasoning a human reviews), plus one Analysis Decision Record per significant choice. Three tracks
in three languages can only agree to the ninth decimal because every rule is written down; your
future self, re-running the analysis on next month's export, depends on the same thing.
objectives: Read a data contract critically: raw columns, cleaning rules and their order, checks and their severities.
Write an analysis plan with hypotheses, competing explanations, metrics, tests and their assumptions, and what would change the decision.
Explain why the primary test is a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test stratified by channel, and what a Simpson's paradox would look like in this funnel.
Draw the pipeline from raw CSVs to `answers.json`, the report and the dashboard, including where it stops on a failed check.
Record decisions as ADRs with options, consequences and the numbers they could move.

steps.title: Read the contract like a reviewer
steps.content_md:
Open `contract/data-contract.yaml` and `contract/questions.md` §2 side by side. For each defect you
noted in Phase 0, find the rule that handles it and the issue counter that reports it. Then answer
three questions in your notes:
1. Why are exact duplicates removed **after** normalising labels and parsing timestamps (step 3)?
   *(Hint: `DESKTOP` and `desktop` are the same session.)*
2. Why does a conflicting `session_id` lose **all** of its rows instead of keeping the first?
3. Which checks are `error` and which `warn`, and what is the difference for the business? An
   `error` means a number would be wrong (duplicate ids, an unknown device); a `warn` means a number
   is less certain (more unknown channels than usual).

steps.title: Check two rules by hand on the tiny fixture
steps.content_md:
`contract/fixtures/tiny/` has 14 sessions. Open `sessions.csv` and apply rules 1-5 of §2 with a pen
(or a spreadsheet). Compare your counts with `issues` in `contract/fixtures/tiny-expected.json`. If
you disagree, re-read the rule: the fixture is the contract's executable example, and the unit tests
in Phase 3 hold every track to it.

steps.title: Hypotheses and competing explanations
steps.content_md:
Copy `spec/analysis-plan.md` (the template is already there) and write:
- **H1 (Head of Product):** the mobile checkout loses buyers: purchase given checkout is lower on mobile.
- **H2 (traffic mix):** mobile gets more traffic from channels that convert less; within a channel,
  mobile is no worse. This would make the overall gap a mix effect (a Simpson's paradox).
- **H3 (basket size):** mobile buyers buy as often but spend less per order.

For each, write the metric and the result that would support or refute it. Notice that H1 and H2 can
both be partly true; the plan must be able to tell "partly" apart.

steps.title: Choose the tests and say why
steps.content_md:
| Question | Test | Why this one | Report |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q3 | two-proportion z test (pooled) | two independent proportions, large counts | difference + unpooled 95 % CI, z, p |
| Q4 | Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel, strata = channel | one common odds ratio across 2×2 tables, adjusting for channel | MH odds ratio + Robins-Breslow-Greenland 95 % CI, p; the crude OR next to it |
| Q5 | Welch's t test | means of skewed order values, unequal variances | difference + 95 % CI, df, p |

Write the assumptions of each (independence of sessions, enough events per stratum, no continuity
correction) and the formula reference in `contract/questions.md` §4. The CMH test is the **one**
primary test of the decision rule; the others are context. Writing that down now is your protection
against reporting whichever test "worked".

steps.title: Draw the pipeline
steps.content_md:
Add a Mermaid diagram to the plan: raw CSVs (text) → cleaning rules (with issue counts) → contract
checks (`error` → exit 3, no output) → funnel tables → tests → opportunity → decision →
`answers.json` → report / dashboard / AI narrator. GitHub renders Mermaid in Markdown, so the diagram
lives next to the text and is reviewed in the same pull request.

steps.title: Write the ADRs
steps.content_md:
Use `spec/adr/0000-template.md`. Five decisions deserve a record:
1. **Read everything as text**; the cleaning rules decide every type (no type guessing by the CSV reader).
2. **Adjust for channel with CMH** as the single primary test.
3. **One output contract for three tracks** (`answers.json` + schema), golden answers and parity to 1e-9.
4. **Contract checks with severities**: `error` stops the run (exit 3), `warn` is reported.
5. **The AI narrator sees facts, not data**: numbered aggregates in, guardrails out, a deterministic
   template when the model is absent, slow or wrong.

Each ADR names at least two real alternatives (pandas' type inference; a logistic regression with a
channel term; one track only; warnings only; letting the model read `answers.json` directly) and
the consequence you accept.

ai_prompts.title: Review my data contract
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is a data contract for an e-commerce funnel export: <paste contract/data-contract.yaml> and the
cleaning rules: <paste contract/questions.md §2>. Review it like a senior analytics engineer: which
rule order changes the result, which defect is not covered, which check has the wrong severity, and
what would silently corrupt revenue. Quote the rule for every point.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: testing each claimed gap against the tiny fixture or the rules text (an assistant may claim a defect is "not handled" when §2 handles it), and turning any real gap into an issue rather than an edit to the contract in this phase.

ai_prompts.title: Explain CMH and Simpson's paradox with my numbers' shape
ai_prompts.prompt:
I compare a conversion step between mobile and desktop users, stratified by acquisition channel
(email, organic, paid_social, unknown). Explain, with a small made-up example of 2x2 tables, how the
Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio can differ from the crude odds ratio, and how an overall gap can vanish or
reverse within every channel (Simpson's paradox). Then list the assumptions of the CMH test.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: recomputing the assistant's made-up example by hand (the MH odds ratio is Σ(a·d/n) / Σ(b·c/n)); assistants often get the arithmetic of their own examples wrong. Check the assumptions against `contract/questions.md` §4 and a statistics reference.

ai_prompts.title: Draft an ADR, then argue against it
ai_prompts.prompt:

<"read every raw CSV as text and parse types in the cleaning rules">. Context: <three tracks must
agree to 1e-9; exports have amounts like "₹1,299.00" and two date formats>. Give two real
alternatives. Then write the strongest argument against the decision.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking the alternatives are real options with real costs (not straw men), and that the consequences mention a number that could move. Keep the counter-argument in the ADR's consequences if it is valid.

`spec/analysis-plan.md`: hypotheses H1-H3, metrics, tests with assumptions, the pipeline diagram, what would change the decision, threats to validity.
At least five ADRs in `spec/adr/` (0001-0005).
A merged PR with a green CI run and an `AI_LOG.md` entry.

quiz.q: Why are exact duplicate sessions removed after normalising labels and parsing dates?
options: It is faster
`DESKTOP` vs `desktop` or `2026-01-05 14:03:00` vs `05/01/2026 14:03` are the same session written differently; comparing raw text would keep both
Because the contract checks need it
Duplicates cannot be found in raw text
quiz.explanation: Order matters. Normalise first, then compare; otherwise "duplicates" depend on formatting accidents and the counts differ between tracks.

quiz.q: Two rows share a `session_id` but have different devices. What does the contract do, and why?
options: Keep the first row
Keep the row with the latest timestamp
Drop all rows of that id and count it: there is no way to know which row is true, and guessing would bias the device comparison
Stop the pipeline
quiz.explanation: A conflicting id is ambiguous evidence. Dropping it (and counting it in `sessions_conflicting_ids`) is honest and reproducible; the count is small enough not to matter, and the check proves it.

quiz.q: What makes the CMH test the right primary test here?
options: It is the most famous test
It compares mobile vs desktop within each channel and combines the strata into one odds ratio, removing confounding by channel mix
It works without any data cleaning
It always gives smaller p-values
quiz.explanation: The question is "is mobile worse for comparable users?". Stratifying by the known confounder and pooling with Mantel-Haenszel answers exactly that; the crude odds ratio is reported alongside to show how much the mix mattered.

quiz.q: Mobile carts less often overall, but within every channel mobile carts as often as desktop. What is this?
options: A bug in the funnel
A Simpson's paradox: the aggregate gap comes from the channel mix, not from the device
Proof the checkout is broken
Regression to the mean
quiz.explanation: When groups have different mixes of a variable that affects the outcome, the aggregate can disagree with every subgroup. The `simpson` section of answers.json reports both so a reader sees it.

quiz.q: An `error` check fails. What happens?
options: A warning is printed and the analysis continues
The pipeline stops with exit code 3 before writing answers.json: a wrong number is worse than no number
The failing rows are deleted automatically
The check is retried
quiz.explanation: `error` checks guard invariants that, if broken, make results wrong (duplicate ids, unknown devices). `warn` checks report degraded certainty and let the run finish.

quiz.q: Why does the AI narrator get numbered facts instead of answers.json or the raw data?
options: Models cannot read JSON
It is cheaper
Facts are aggregates only (privacy), and numbering them lets guardrails check every citation and every number the model writes
Because the template needs them
quiz.explanation: The smaller and more structured the model's input, the easier it is to verify its output. ADR-0005 records this, and Phase 6 implements the guardrails.

recap: A data contract makes cleaning rules, checks and severities machine-checkable; the order of rules changes numbers.
An analysis plan fixes hypotheses, metrics, tests and the decision before the data can influence them.
Stratification (CMH) addresses a known confounder, and Simpson's paradox is what it protects against.
ADRs make analysis decisions reviewable: alternatives, consequences, the numbers they move.
A tiny hand-checkable fixture is the executable example of the contract.

phases.title: Implementation in five milestones
phases.heading: Phase 3 · Implementation in five milestones: load, clean, explore, test, decide
phases.why_md:
This is where the old guide's "Load and Clean", "Explore" and "Test the Hypothesis" happen, but
**test-first**: for every rule and every formula a test already says what the right answer is, on a
fixture small enough to check by hand. You switch the tests on one milestone at a time, watch them
fail, and make them pass. By the end, your track turns the raw export into an `answers.json` that the
decision rule reads, and your report (notebook, SQL report or R Markdown) tells the story from it.
Nothing is copied from an assistant without a test agreeing with it.
objectives: Load raw CSVs as text and implement the cleaning rules of `contract/questions.md` §2 in order, counting every row each rule changes.
Implement the data-contract checks and stop the pipeline on a failing `error` check.
Build the session funnel by device, channel and week, and find the Simpson's paradox in the cart step.
Implement the two-proportion z test, the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test with the Robins-Breslow-Greenland interval and Welch's t test, and match hand-computed cases to 1e-9.
Size the opportunity, apply the decision rule and write a report that runs top to bottom.

steps.title: M1 · Load and clean
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **"Phase 3 M1 - load the raw export as text"** and **"Phase 3 M1 - cleaning rules and the
issue counts"**. Implement in the order of §2: users, sessions (steps 1-8), events, orders. Rules
that are easy to get subtly wrong, and which the tests pin:
- **Timestamps:** exactly two formats; `05/01/2026 14:03` is 5 January. An impossible date is a bad
  timestamp, not a guess.
- **Amounts:** whole **paise** as integers (`₹1,299.00` → 129900). Floats for money drift; integer
  paise sum exactly in every language.
- **Duplicates:** exact duplicates after normalisation keep one row; a conflicting id loses all rows.
- **The join trap:** joining orders to sessions on a key that is not unique multiplies revenue.
  Check uniqueness before every join and compare row counts before and after.

orders.merge(sessions[["session_id", "device"]], on="session_id", how="inner", validate="many_to_one")

steps.title: M2 · Contract checks
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **"Phase 3 M2 - data-contract checks"**. Each check type is a small function (or SQL
template) that returns the failing-row count and, for ratio checks, the observed ratio. Checks run in
contract order on the clean tables; `raise_on_errors` stops with a contract error when an `error`
check fails, and the command line turns that into exit code 3. Run your pipeline on the real export
now (`make run`): it should stop at the first unimplemented step, not with a wrong number.

steps.title: M3 · Explore: the funnel by device, channel and week
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **"Phase 3 M3 - funnel by device, channel and week"**. This is the old "Explore" step,
made precise: a session reaches a step only if it reached the previous one; a purchase is a session
with an order. Before moving on, look at your own numbers on the real export:
1. Where does mobile diverge from desktop: everywhere, or at one step?
2. Split by channel. Does mobile carry more `paid_social` traffic? Is mobile's cart rate lower
   *within* each channel, or only overall?
3. Plot sessions and conversion per week. A break or a backfill would invalidate any comparison
   across the period.

Write two or three candidate explanations, ranked by how well this evidence supports them, in your
report. You should find that the overall cart gap is mostly **channel mix**, while the payment step
is worse on mobile within every channel.

steps.title: M4 · Test the hypothesis
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **"Phase 3 M4 - two-proportion z, CMH and Welch tests"**. Implement the formulas of §4.
`contract/fixtures/stats-cases.json` has hand-computed cases (including a stratum with a zero cell
and unequal variances) that every track must match to 1e-9.

<!-- track:python -->
Use the libraries, then prove them against the cases: `statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportions_ztest`,
`statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables.StratifiedTable` (`oddsratio_pooled`, `test_null_odds(correction=False)`)
and `scipy.stats.ttest_ind(equal_var=False)`. Check which defaults differ from the contract (the CI of
the z test is unpooled; the RBG variance is computed explicitly).
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:sql -->

quiz.q: Why are amounts stored as whole paise (integers) instead of rupees (floats)?
options: Integers use less memory
Integer sums are exact in every language, so revenue totals agree across tracks; floats accumulate rounding error
The contract forbids decimals
Paise are easier to read
quiz.explanation: Money in floating point drifts (0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3). Integer paise make `revenue_paise` identical in pandas, DuckDB and R, and conversion to rupees happens only when a mean is computed.

quiz.q: After joining orders to sessions, revenue is 7 % higher than the sum of orders. What is the most likely cause?
options: Refunds were removed
The session key was not unique on the session side, so some orders were duplicated by the join
The sample rate was applied twice
Orders without checkout were kept
quiz.explanation: A many-to-many join silently multiplies rows. Check uniqueness first, and use `validate="many_to_one"` (pandas) or `relationship = "many-to-one"` (dplyr) so the join fails instead.

quiz.q: Mobile's cart rate is lower overall but not within channels; its payment rate is lower within every channel. What does the evidence support?
options: The whole mobile funnel is broken
Nothing: the results contradict each other
The cart gap is mostly channel mix, while the payment step is a genuine mobile gap among comparable users
Desktop users are lying
quiz.explanation: Stratifying separates the two effects. That is exactly why `decision.reasons` can contain both `adjusted_payment_gap_significant` and `aggregate_cart_gap_is_channel_mix`.

quiz.q: Your z-test p-value differs from the golden file in the 4th digit. What is the first thing to check?
options: Whether the golden file is outdated
Whether your library applies a default the contract does not (for example a continuity correction, or a pooled variance where the contract uses unpooled)
Whether your computer is 32-bit
Whether the sample is too small
quiz.explanation: Library defaults are the most common cause of "almost equal" statistics. The contract writes the formula; `stats-cases.json` shows the exact expected values.

quiz.q: The CMH p-value is far below 0.05 and the uplift is ₹16 lakh a month. What does the decision rule say?
options: Rebuild the checkout: the gap is highly significant
Run a targeted experiment: the gap is real but worth less than the ₹25 lakh rebuild threshold
Do not rebuild: the gap is not significant
Collect more data
quiz.explanation: Significance says the gap is unlikely to be noise; the threshold says whether closing it pays for a rebuild. An experiment on the payment step tests fixes at a fraction of the cost.

quiz.q: Why must the report run top to bottom from a clean state?
options: Jupyter and R Markdown require it
Cells run out of order (or objects left in a session) can produce results the code no longer reproduces; a clean run is the only proof
It makes the report shorter
CI cannot read notebooks otherwise
quiz.explanation: Hidden state is the classic notebook bug. `make report` restarts from nothing; Phase 5 makes CI do the same on every push.

Defensive cleaning: text-first loading, counted rules, integer money, uniqueness before joins.
Exploration with a purpose: funnel by device, channel and week, and how stratification exposes a Simpson's paradox.
Three hypothesis tests implemented exactly, including the library defaults that silently change results.
A mechanical decision rule, a parity check against golden answers, and a report that runs from scratch.

phases.title: Testing the analysis: golden answers, invariants, parity, coverage
phases.heading: Phase 4 · Testing the analysis: golden answers, invariants, parity, coverage
phases.why_md:
Unit tests on a 14-session fixture prove each rule. They do not prove that the analysis of the real
export is right, that nothing is double-counted, or that a broken export is refused. Analysts rarely
test their work this way, which is why "the numbers changed and nobody knows why" is so common. In
this phase you switch on three kinds of **data tests**: golden answers (the whole `answers.json` on
the real export), invariants (properties that must hold for *any* export, such as "devices add up to
all"), and contract violations (a corrupted export must stop the run). You add a coverage gate, break
the analysis on purpose to see the tests catch it, and compare your track with another one.
objectives: Explain the difference between unit tests, golden tests, invariants and contract-violation tests, and what each one cannot catch.
Un-pend and pass the data tests of your track on the real export.
Read a parity report and trace a difference to a rule.
Break the analysis on purpose (a join, a rule order, a default) and show which test fails.
Enforce an 85 % line-coverage gate and explain what coverage does not tell you.

steps.title: Know the layers you already have
steps.content_md:
| Layer | Where | Catches | Misses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit | `tests/unit`, tiny fixture | a wrong rule or formula | interactions on real data, scale |
| Golden | `tests/data/test_golden*` | any change of any number on the real export | *why* it changed |
| Invariants | `tests/data/test_invariants*` | double counting, lost rows, impossible statistics | a consistently wrong formula |
| Contract violations | `tests/data/test_contract_violations*` | a broken export analysed silently | a new defect type the contract does not know |
| Parity | `scripts/parity.py` | a track-specific bug or an ambiguous rule | an error all tracks share |

steps.title: Read the invariants
steps.content_md:
Open the invariants file of your track and explain each test in one sentence in your notes. The most
useful one is *rows removed + rows kept = rows read*: for every table, the issue counts plus the clean
row count must add up to the raw row count. It turns the cleaning log into an equation, so a rule
that drops rows without counting them fails immediately.

steps.title: Break it on purpose
steps.content_md:
Make each change on a scratch branch, run `make coverage`, write down which test failed, then revert:
1. Join orders to sessions **before** removing conflicting session ids (revenue multiplies).
2. Remove exact duplicates **before** normalising labels (the duplicate count drops).
3. Use the library default with a continuity correction for the z test (the p-value moves).
4. Count a purchase for an order without a checkout (the funnel grows at the last step).

If a change breaks no test, you found a gap: write an invariant or a unit test that catches it.

agree are strong evidence that the rules are unambiguous and the formulas right; it is the
analysis equivalent of a second pair of eyes.

quiz.q: The golden test passes. What does that prove?
options: That the analysis is correct
That your answers.json equals the agreed reference on this export; the reference could share an error with you, which is why invariants and independent tracks exist
That the code has no bugs
That the next export will be analysed correctly
quiz.explanation: A golden test pins behaviour; it does not prove truth. Parity across three independent implementations and invariants make a shared mistake much less likely.

quiz.q: Which invariant catches a join that multiplies revenue?
options: The funnel never grows
Rows removed plus rows kept equals rows read: duplicated orders make the clean count larger than the raw count minus the removed rows
No error check fails
Statistics are well formed
quiz.explanation: A many-to-many join creates rows that no rule removed and no raw file contained, so the cleaning equation stops balancing (and the golden revenue changes too).

quiz.q: You append a session with channel `referral` to a copy of the export. What must happen?
options: It is counted as `unknown`
It is silently dropped
The `sessions.channel.accepted` error check fails and the run stops with exit code 3
The dashboard shows a warning
quiz.explanation: An unknown value is a contract change, not a cleaning problem. Stopping forces a human to decide, and Phase 7 shows what happens when a real refresh does exactly this.

quiz.q: Coverage is 99 %. What does that not tell you?
options: Which lines ran during the tests
Whether the assertions check the right values: a line can run in a test that asserts nothing useful
Whether the gate passes
Which files are untested
quiz.explanation: Coverage measures execution, not verification. The "break it on purpose" exercise is the real test of your tests.

quiz.q: Parity reports one difference: `$.data_quality.issues.sessions_exact_duplicates: 351 != 349`. Most likely cause?
options: A floating-point error
A different rule order or normalisation before deduplication (for example comparing raw labels)
The golden file is corrupted
The sample rate
quiz.explanation: Integer differences in issue counts point at rule logic, never at floating point. Re-read §2 step 3: duplicates are compared after normalising labels and parsing timestamps.

quiz.q: Why add a finding-level test ("the adjusted payment OR is below 1 with a CI excluding 1")?
options: To increase coverage
So a change of the story (not just a digit) fails loudly, with a message a stakeholder would understand
Because the golden test is not enough to run CI
Because statsmodels requires it
quiz.explanation: Golden tests fail on any change, including harmless ones after a contract update. A finding-level test says which conclusion is at risk.

recap: Four layers of tests for an analysis, and what each layer cannot catch.
Invariants that turn the cleaning log into equations.
Mutation-style testing: break the analysis on purpose and make sure a test notices.
Parity across independent implementations as a review tool.
Coverage as a floor, not a proof.

phases.title: CI with GitHub Actions
phases.heading: Phase 5 · CI with GitHub Actions
phases.why_md:
"It runs on my laptop" is the analyst's version of "works on my machine". A notebook that only runs
in your kernel, with packages only you installed, is not reproducible; neither is a report someone
re-ran "with a small fix". Continuous integration runs the whole analysis from a clean checkout on
every push: lint, unit tests, data tests with a coverage gate, the report executed top to bottom,
and a **parity job** that compares every track's `answers.json` with the golden answers. Every PR now
carries proof that the numbers did not change, or a red X that says exactly which one did.
objectives: Explain workflows, jobs, steps, runners, triggers, matrices, caches, artifacts and reusable workflows.
Replace the starter CI with a pipeline that runs only the tracks whose files changed, through one reusable workflow.
Execute the notebook / SQL report / R Markdown report in CI and upload it as an artifact.
Pass `answers.json` between jobs with artifacts and fail the build when tracks disagree with the golden answers.
Protect `main` with a required check and read a red run quickly.

steps.title: Read the starter workflow
steps.content_md:
Open `.github/workflows/ci.yml` next to [GitHub Actions explained](github-actions-explained.md) §1-§5.
It has one job with a matrix of three tracks: each gets a fresh Ubuntu runner, sets up Python (or R
with `r-lib/actions`), installs, lints and runs the unit tests. Find in the YAML: the triggers, the
matrix, the cache and the `working-directory` default. Note what it does **not** do: data tests,
coverage, reports, parity.

steps.title: One reusable workflow for all tracks
steps.content_md:
Create `.github/workflows/reusable-track-ci.yml` (`on: workflow_call`, input `track`). Because every
track has the same Makefile targets, the steps are identical: install, lint, test, coverage, run,
report. Only the setup differs:

<!-- track:python -->
`actions/setup-python@v5` with `cache: pip` keyed on `tracks/python/requirements-dev.txt`; `make
report` executes the notebook with `jupyter nbconvert --execute`, which fails the job on any cell error.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:sql -->

steps.title: The main workflow: path filters, parity, dashboard, ci-ok
steps.content_md:
Replace `ci.yml` with the full pipeline (compare with the reference at `phase-5-end`):
1. `changes` uses `dorny/paths-filter` to decide what changed: a track folder, `dashboard/`, docs, or
   shared files (`contract/`, `data/`, `scripts/`, workflows). Shared changes run everything.
2. `contract` checks the shared files: `generate_data.py --check`, the golden answers against the
   schema, `shellcheck`, and `build-cms.py --check`.
3. `python`, `sql`, `r` call the reusable workflow.
4. `parity` downloads every `answers-*` artifact and runs `scripts/parity.py` against the golden
   file of the same export. It writes the result to the job summary.
5. `dashboard` lints and tests the dashboard (its AI narrator is tested against a fake LLM server, no key).
6. `ci-ok` depends on everything and fails if any needed job failed: the one check to require.

steps.title: Validate locally, then push
steps.content_md:
```bash
pipx run actionlint            # or: brew install actionlint / go install …
python3 scripts/build-cms.py --check
git switch -c ci/full-pipeline && git add .github && git commit -m "ci: reusable track workflow, parity and dashboard jobs, ci-ok"
git push -u origin ci/full-pipeline
```
Open the PR and watch the Actions tab: the first R run takes longer (the package cache is cold); the
second is much faster. Download the `report-<track>` artifact and open the executed report.

steps.title: Protect main
steps.content_md:
In your fork: **Settings → Branches → Add branch ruleset** (or classic protection) for `main`:
require a pull request, require the status check **`ci-ok`**, require branches to be up to date,
block force pushes. From now on a PR that changes a number without changing the golden file (with a
reason in the contract) cannot be merged.

steps.title: Make it fail once
steps.content_md:

read the red run: which job failed, which step, which JSON path? Practise going from the red X to the
cause in under two minutes ([GitHub Actions explained](github-actions-explained.md) §16). Then revert.

for each job what would make it fail: <paste .github/workflows/ci.yml>. Then list what it would cost
in minutes per push and how the path filter changes that.

quiz.q: Why do the three tracks share one reusable workflow?
options: GitHub allows only one workflow per repository
The steps are identical because every track has the same Makefile targets; one definition means one place to fix and no drift between tracks
Reusable workflows are faster
Matrix builds cannot run R
quiz.explanation: The Makefile is the interface; CI calls `make install lint test coverage run report` in any track. Only the toolchain setup differs, and that is a few `if:` lines.

quiz.q: How does the parity job get the other jobs' answers.json?
options: It reads them from the runner's disk
It re-runs the three pipelines
Each track job uploads `answers-<track>` as an artifact; the parity job downloads them
Through a database service
quiz.explanation: Every job runs on a fresh machine. Artifacts are the way to pass files between jobs (and to let humans download reports).

quiz.q: Why execute the notebook or R Markdown report in CI?
options: To make the run longer
To prove the report runs top to bottom from a clean checkout with the pinned dependencies, so its numbers are reproducible
Because GitHub displays notebooks
To generate the golden answers
quiz.explanation: A report that fails or depends on hidden state fails CI. The executed report is attached to the run as evidence.

quiz.q: Why is `ci-ok`, not every job, the required status check?
options: Required checks cannot be reusable workflows
With path filters, some jobs are legitimately skipped; one aggregator job that fails on any failure or cancellation (and accepts skips) gives branch protection one stable name
It is cheaper
GitHub limits required checks to one
quiz.explanation: A required check that is skipped never reports, so the PR would wait forever. The aggregator turns "all needed jobs passed or were skipped" into one result.

quiz.q: What does `use-public-rspm: true` in `setup-r` do?
options: Uses a public R mirror for documentation
Installs binary packages from Posit Public Package Manager instead of compiling them from source, which cuts minutes from each run
Makes the R job public
Disables the cache
quiz.explanation: Compiling dplyr and friends from source on Linux takes a long time; binaries for the runner's Ubuntu version install in seconds.

quiz.q: A PR changes a cleaning rule and CI fails only in the parity job. What does that mean?
options: CI is flaky
The rule change moved at least one number: either the change is a bug, or it is intended and needs a contract change and new golden answers agreed by all tracks
The artifact upload failed
The golden file must be deleted
quiz.explanation: Parity makes number changes visible and deliberate. An intended change updates `questions.md` (with a version bump), all tracks and the golden file in one reviewed PR.

One reusable workflow driven by a uniform Makefile interface across Python, SQL and R.
Reports executed in CI and attached as artifacts; reproducibility as an automatic check.
Artifacts between jobs and a parity job that guards every number.
Branch protection with an aggregator check, and fast diagnosis of a red run.

phases.heading: Phase 6 · Dashboard, AI narrator, Docker and delivery
phases.why_md:
An analysis that lives in a notebook reaches the people who open notebooks. The Head of Product
needs the recommendation, the evidence and the caveat on one screen, and a memo to forward. In this
phase you ship the old "Present" step as a product: the shared **Streamlit dashboard** reads your
`answers.json`, an optional **AI narrator** writes the summary under strict guardrails, and
everything runs in **Docker** with one command, so anyone can reproduce the numbers without
installing pandas, DuckDB or R. A version tag publishes the images; that is release **v1.0.0**.
objectives: Run the dashboard on your own track's `answers.json` and explain what each tab shows.
Explain the narrator's design (facts in, guardrails out, template fallback) and see each guardrail reject a bad summary.
Read the Dockerfiles: few layers, non-root user, read-only file system, no secrets in the image.
Run every track's pipeline and the parity check in containers, and smoke-test the dashboard, also with the AI provider down.
Release v1.0.0: CHANGELOG, tag, images on GHCR, and (optionally) a free public deployment.

steps.title: The dashboard on your answers
steps.content_md:
```bash
cd dashboard
make install
make run ANSWERS=../tracks/<python|sql|r>/out/answers.json     # http://localhost:18120 by default (PORT=…)
```
`make prepare` validates the answers against the schema, then writes `static/answers.json`,
`static/narrative.json` (the summary) and `static/onepager.md` (the decision memo). The app only
displays those files: it never sees raw data. Walk through the tabs and check three numbers against
your report. Any track's answers work, because they are identical.

steps.title: The AI narrator and its guardrails
steps.content_md:
Read `funnellens_dashboard/facts.py` and `narrator.py`. The model receives numbered facts
(`[F1] Mobile is 69.2% of sessions but 60.6% of revenue.`) and must cite them. `validate()` rejects a
summary that is longer than 900 characters, cites an unknown fact, contains a number that is not a
correct rounding of a fact value, mentions a date that is not in the facts, uses causal words
("caused", "proves", "guaranteed"), or omits the recommendation or the caveat. On any rejection,
timeout or HTTP error, the deterministic template is used and the reason is shown.

Try it with a real model if you have one (all optional, nothing is paid):
```bash
# a local Ollama (no key):  ollama pull llama3.2
AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1 LLM_MODEL=llama3.2 make prepare ANSWERS=…
cat static/narrative.json        # source "llm", or "template" with the reason it was rejected
```
Then read `tests/test_narrator.py`: every guardrail has a test against a fake LLM server, so CI
needs no key. Write down one way a summary could still mislead (emphasis, omission) that no
guardrail catches; a human review of the memo stays part of the process.

steps.title: The Dockerfiles
steps.content_md:
Open `tracks/<yours>/Dockerfile` and `dashboard/Dockerfile`. They share four habits:
1. **Few layers:** a `FROM scratch AS src` stage collects the files; the final stage installs the
   dependencies in one `RUN` (with a bind mount, so `requirements.txt` is not even copied) and copies
   the code in one `COPY`. Small images, fast rebuilds.
2. **Non-root:** user `10001`, created in the same `RUN`.
3. **No data, no secrets in the image:** the export is mounted read-only at run time; the AI key, if
   any, is an environment variable.
4. **The dashboard image bakes answers:** its first stage runs the Python pipeline on the committed
   export, so the image starts with real answers; `ANSWERS_PATH` can point to another track's output.

<!-- track:r -->
The R image installs R and the tidyverse from Debian's `r-base-core` and `r-cran-*` packages (binary,
one `apt-get` layer), on the same slim Python base as the other images: about 300 MB instead of the
1-2 GB of a full `rocker/tidyverse` image.

steps.title: Compose: pipelines, parity and the dashboard
steps.content_md:
```bash
cp .env.example .env                                   # optional: ports, AI provider
docker compose --profile pipelines build
for t in python sql r; do docker compose --profile pipelines run --rm "$t"; done
docker compose --profile pipelines run --rm --no-deps parity        # IDENTICAL x3
docker compose up -d --wait dashboard                               # http://localhost:8501
scripts/smoke-test.sh http://localhost:8501
```
The pipelines run read-only, non-root, and write to a named volume that the dashboard can read
(`ANSWERS_PATH=/answers/r/answers.json docker compose up -d dashboard` shows the R track's answers).

steps.title: Smoke test with the AI provider down
steps.content_md:
```bash
AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://10.255.255.1:9/v1 LLM_TIMEOUT_MS=1500 \
  docker compose up -d --wait --force-recreate dashboard
EXPECT_FALLBACK=true scripts/smoke-test.sh http://localhost:8501   # 10 checks, incl. "fell back to the template"
docker compose --profile pipelines down -v
```
The dashboard must work, and say why the summary is the template, when the model is unreachable.

steps.title: CI builds the images; a tag publishes them
steps.content_md:
Compare `.github/workflows/ci.yml` at `phase-6-end` with Phase 5: a `docker` job builds the four
images, runs the three pipelines and the parity check in containers, and runs both smoke tests.
`.github/workflows/deploy.yml` runs on a version tag: it pushes
`ghcr.io/<owner>/funnellens-{dashboard,python,sql,r}:<version>` with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`
(see [GitHub Actions explained](github-actions-explained.md) §12).

**Optional free deployment.** Render can run the dashboard image for free (it sleeps when idle):
create a *Web Service* from the image `ghcr.io/<owner>/funnellens-dashboard:latest` (make the package
public first), copy its *Deploy Hook* URL into the repository secret `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` of an
environment named `production`, and its URL into the variable `RENDER_APP_URL`. Without them the
deploy job succeeds with a notice. Keep `AI_PROVIDER=offline` on a public deployment unless you set a
spending limit on the key.

steps.title: Release v1.0.0
steps.content_md:
1. Move the `Unreleased` notes in `CHANGELOG.md` to `## [1.0.0]` with today's date.
2. Write `docs/runbook.md`: how to re-run the analysis on a new export, what each exit code means,
   what to do when a check fails, how to switch the narrator off.
3. Forward the memo (`static/onepager.md`, also downloadable from the dashboard) to the Head of
   Product: recommendation, evidence, caveat, next step (the experiment).
4. Tag and push: `git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "FunnelLens v1.0.0" && git push origin v1.0.0`.

ai_prompts.title: Try to break the guardrails

Here is the system prompt and the numbered facts of an AI summary feature: <paste SYSTEM_PROMPT from
narrator.py and the facts block from static/onepager.md>. Write five summaries that a careless or
manipulated model might produce, each violating a different rule (an invented number, a wrong
rounding, a causal claim, a missing caveat, a fake citation), and one that is misleading but follows
every rule.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: feeding each summary to `validate()` (a quick test with the fake LLM fixture) and checking that the five are rejected for the reason you expect. Add a test for any that passes, and write the "misleading but valid" one into your notes as a known limitation.

ai_prompts.title: Review my Dockerfile
ai_prompts.prompt:
Review this Dockerfile for a data pipeline image: <paste>. Check: layer count and order for cache
efficiency, the final image size, running as non-root, secrets or data baked into layers, and whether
the container works with a read-only root file system. Suggest changes with the reason for each, and
do not change the base image.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: rebuilding and comparing `docker image ls` sizes and `docker history` layer counts before and after, running the container with `--read-only`, and checking `docker run --rm <image> id -u` prints 10001.

ai_prompts.title: Write the decision memo
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is the one-page decision memo generated from my analysis: <paste static/onepager.md>. Rewrite
it for a Head of Product who has 2 minutes: recommendation first, three supporting facts with their
intervals, one sentence on what the data cannot show, and the next step. Use only numbers that appear
in the memo, and keep every number exactly as written.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking every number in the rewrite against the memo character by character, and rejecting any causal phrasing ("the checkout causes"). Keep the original as the attachment: the rewrite is a cover note, not a replacement.

quiz.q: Why does the narrator receive numbered facts instead of answers.json?
options: The model cannot read JSON
Facts are short aggregates whose exact values are known, so every citation and every number in the summary can be checked against them
It is required by the OpenAI API
Facts are encrypted
quiz.explanation: The guardrails work because the input is small and structured: a number in the output must be a correct rounding of a fact value, and a citation must name a fact that exists.

quiz.q: The model is unreachable. What does the dashboard show?
options: An error page
Nothing until the model is back
The deterministic template summary, marked as such, with the reason the AI was not used
The last summary the model wrote
quiz.explanation: The template is computed from the same facts and always passes the guardrails, so the product works offline and the fallback is visible, never silent.

quiz.q: A model writes "The checkout caused a ₹16.3 lakh monthly loss [F7]". Why is it rejected?
options: The number is wrong
The citation is unknown
"caused" is a causal claim the observational data cannot support
It is too long
quiz.explanation: The number and citation may be correct; the claim is not. Causal language is banned because only an experiment could establish it.

quiz.q: Why does each image install its dependencies and create the user in a single `RUN`?
options: Docker allows only one `RUN`
Each instruction adds a layer; fewer layers make smaller images and faster pulls, and the dependency layer stays cached when only the code changes
It makes the image run faster
It hides the user from `docker inspect`
quiz.explanation: Layer discipline matters on every laptop and CI runner. Code is copied last so changing it does not invalidate the expensive dependency layer.

quiz.q: Why are the pipeline containers run with a read-only file system and as user 10001?
options: Docker requires it
Least privilege: a compromised or buggy container cannot modify its own code or write outside the output volume, and does not run as root
It makes the analysis faster
The CSVs are read-only
quiz.explanation: An analysis container needs to read the export and write one folder. Everything else is denied by default.

quiz.q: What does pushing the tag `v1.0.0` trigger?
options: Nothing: tags are only labels
A new golden file
The deploy workflow: the four images are pushed to GHCR with the version, and the optional Render deploy runs if configured
A merge of `solution` into `main`
quiz.explanation: `on: push: tags: ["v*.*.*"]` ties releases to tags, so the image version always matches the code that produced it.

phases.title: Data refresh, monitoring and a post-mortem
phases.heading: Phase 7 · Data refresh, monitoring and a post-mortem
phases.why_md:
The memo went out; the Head of Product approved the experiment and asked for the numbers again on
the **August export (2026-08)**. You run the same pipeline on the new folder and it stops:
`data contract violated: sessions.channel.accepted (878 rows)`. That is the contract doing its job.
Behind it are three real-world changes: marketing launched a **referral** programme, orders now carry
a **payment method**, and app release **8.14** silently lost about 70% of mobile checkout events
for one week. In analytics, the dangerous failures are the silent ones. This phase adds a versioned
contract, data-quality **monitoring** over time, an incident **post-mortem**, and release **v1.1.0**,
without breaking anyone who reads v1.0 answers.
objectives: Diagnose a failing pipeline from its exit code and the failing check, and decide whether the data or the contract is wrong.
Evolve the data contract with a version (1.0.0 → 1.1.0), keep the old version, and keep the answers schema backward compatible.
Add monitoring: freshness, weekly metrics against their median, anomalies; report them without stopping the run.
Exclude a week of broken tracking explicitly, with a post-mortem, and quantify what it changes.
Prove backward compatibility: v1.1 reproduces the v1.0 golden file on 2026-06, and the v1.0 dashboard reads v1.1 answers.

steps.title: Run v1.0 on the new export
steps.content_md:
```bash
git switch -c my-phase-7 phase-6-end
ls data/raw/2026-08 && cat data/README.md | head -40      # the new data dictionary
cd tracks/<yours> && make run DATA=../../data/raw/2026-08; echo "exit $?"
```
Exit code 3 (contract violated) and the check id `sessions.channel.accepted` with 878 rows. Query the
rows (`SELECT channel, count(*) …`): they are all `referral`, a new, legitimate channel. The data is

steps.content_md:
Run v1.1 on 2026-08 **without** excluding any week first (`exclude_weeks: []`). Every check passes
except one warning: `orders.without_checkout.ratio` (113 orders, 3.3%). Then look at
`answers.monitoring.anomalies`:

| week | metric | value | median | deviation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-W31 | mobile_checkout_given_cart | 0.107 | 0.534 | −80% |

Mobile users did not stop paying (orders exist without a checkout event: that is the warning).
The **tracking** broke. The release notes confirm it: app 8.14 shipped on Monday of W31 and the
hotfix 8.14.1 the next Monday. Weekly monitoring turned a vague warning into a dated cause.

steps.content_md:

excluded, no warning, no anomaly. Then write `docs/postmortem-2026-W31.md` in the blameless format
(summary, impact, timeline, root cause, detection, what went well, what went badly, action items
with owners). Quantify the impact on the decision: with W31 left in, the payment-step uplift moves by
about ₹0.2 lakh/month and the recommendation does not change, but the weekly chart shows a false
collapse that a reader could take for a real drop. With W31 excluded, the CMH odds ratio is 0.725
and the uplift ₹14.3 lakh/month: still `run_targeted_experiment`.

options: Remove the failing check
Map unknown channels to `unknown`
Look at the failing rows and find out whether the data or the contract is wrong
Re-run until it passes

quiz.q: Why is the old contract kept in `contract/history/`?
options: Git cannot show old versions

quiz.explanation: A versioned contract is part of the reproducibility of every past result.

options: It was not: warnings can be ignored

The warning threshold was wrong

quiz.q: Why exclude W31 instead of "fixing" its missing checkout events?
options: Excluding is faster

The contract forbids changes to events
W31 is a holiday
quiz.explanation: Exclusion with a post-mortem and a quantified impact is honest; imputation of a broken funnel step would bias the very metric under study.

quiz.q: What does "backward compatible" mean for answers schema 1.1?
options: v1.1 answers are identical to v1.0 answers
It only adds fields: a v1.0 reader still works, and on the old export every v1.0 field keeps its value
It removes unused fields
It can only be read by the v1.1 dashboard

quiz.q: Parity failed on a count during the refresh. What did that reveal?
options: A bug in DuckDB
That one track should be deleted
An ambiguity in the spec: two correct readings gave two numbers, so the spec was clarified
That parity checks are too strict
quiz.explanation: Independent implementations are an excellent spec review. The fix was one sentence in `questions.md`.

recap: A failing contract check is information: diagnose before you change anything.
Versioned contracts and additive schemas keep old results reproducible and old readers working.
Weekly monitoring against a median finds silent tracking failures that row checks miss.
Blameless post-mortems with a quantified impact on the decision.
Independent implementations (parity) expose ambiguities in a spec.

phases.heading: Phase 8 · Retrospective and portfolio
phases.why_md:
Hiring managers for analyst roles see hundreds of Titanic notebooks. What they rarely see is an
analysis that states a decision, survives messy data, quantifies uncertainty, reproduces in CI and
in Docker, and was re-run on new data with an incident handled properly. You have all of that, but
only if a reader can find it in a minute. This phase turns the repository into a portfolio piece:
a README case study, an honest retrospective, and a walkthrough you can give in an interview.
objectives: Present the case study as problem → approach → result → evidence, with numbers and links.
Write a retrospective that separates what worked, what did not, and what you would change.
Explain your statistical choices (CMH, Welch, intervals) and their limits in plain language.
Describe your use of AI precisely: where it helped, where you rejected its output, and how you verified.

Device and channel are related; CMH compares mobile and desktop within each channel, so the channel mix cannot create or hide the gap

legacy_import.title: FunnelLens: Data Analyst Case Study on a Messy E-commerce Funnel
legacy_import.description: Mobile is about 69 % of FunnelLens's sessions but only about 61 % of its revenue, and the Head of Product wants a quarter of engineering time to rebuild the mobile checkout. Over nine phases you find out what the data supports, like a professional analytics team: turn the request into answerable questions with acceptance criteria, write a data contract and an analysis plan with ADRs, then build the analysis test-first in your track: load four deliberately messy CSVs as text, apply documented cleaning rules that count every row they drop, check the contract, build the funnel by device, channel and week, and test the hypothesis three ways (a two-proportion z test, a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test that adjusts for acquisition channel and exposes a Simpson's paradox, and Welch's t test on order values) before sizing the opportunity against the rebuild threshold. Golden answers, invariants and contract-violation tests pin every number, and the Python, SQL and R tracks must agree to 1e-9. CI executes the notebook or R Markdown report and checks parity; a Streamlit dashboard with an optional AI narrator (numbered facts in, guardrails out, a deterministic template as fallback) ships in Docker. Then a data refresh breaks the pipeline on purpose: a new acquisition channel and a broken tracking week lead to a contract version bump, monitoring, a post-mortem and v1.1. Pick Python (pandas, Jupyter), SQL (DuckDB) or R (tidyverse, R Markdown); the data, contract, golden answers and dashboard are shared. Everything runs on a laptop with no paid service and no API key.

steps.title: Phase 0 · Setup and the brief
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
An analysis nobody else can re-run is an opinion with charts. Professional analysts start where
engineers start: a repository that installs with one command, data whose origin you can prove, tests
that say what "right" means, and a log of how AI helped. In this phase you set up the tools for
**one** track, read the brief and the data, run the starter, meet the pending tests and the contract
that will guide you, open your first pull request and start your `AI_LOG.md`. You will not compute a
single number yet, on purpose: first you learn what question is being asked and what the data can say.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Fork the repository **with all branches and tags**, clone it and add the `upstream` remote.
