layer counts before and after, running the container with `--read-only`, and checking `docker run
--rm <image> id -u` prints 10001.

### Prompt 3: Write the decision memo
```text
Here is the one-page decision memo generated from my analysis: <paste static/onepager.md>. Rewrite
it for a Head of Product who has 2 minutes: recommendation first, three supporting facts with their
intervals, one sentence on what the data cannot show, and the next step. Use only numbers that appear
in the memo, and keep every number exactly as written.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking every number in the rewrite against the memo character by
character, and rejecting any causal phrasing ("the checkout causes"). Keep the original as the
attachment: the rewrite is a cover note, not a replacement.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] The dashboard running on your track's answers, locally and in Docker.
- [ ] Notes: the guardrails in your own words, one limitation no guardrail catches.
- [ ] `docker compose` pipelines + parity `IDENTICAL`, smoke test 9/9 and the fallback smoke test 10/10.
- [ ] CI with the Docker job green; `deploy.yml` in place (Render optional).
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` 1.0.0, `docs/runbook.md`, the tag `v1.0.0`, and the memo sent (or drafted).

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Why does the narrator receive numbered facts instead of answers.json?
- [ ] The model cannot read JSON
- [x] Facts are short aggregates whose exact values are known, so every citation and every number in the summary can be checked against them
- [ ] It is required by the OpenAI API
- [ ] Facts are encrypted
> **Answer:** The guardrails work because the input is small and structured: a number in the output must be a correct rounding of a fact value, and a citation must name a fact that exists.

### Q2. The model is unreachable. What does the dashboard show?
- [ ] An error page
- [ ] Nothing until the model is back
- [x] The deterministic template summary, marked as such, with the reason the AI was not used
- [ ] The last summary the model wrote
> **Answer:** The template is computed from the same facts and always passes the guardrails, so the product works offline and the fallback is visible, never silent.

### Q3. A model writes "The checkout caused a ₹16.3 lakh monthly loss [F7]". Why is it rejected?
- [ ] The number is wrong
- [ ] The citation is unknown
- [x] "caused" is a causal claim the observational data cannot support
- [ ] It is too long
> **Answer:** The number and citation may be correct; the claim is not. Causal language is banned because only an experiment could establish it.

### Q4. Why does each image install its dependencies and create the user in a single `RUN`?
- [ ] Docker allows only one `RUN`
- [x] Each instruction adds a layer; fewer layers make smaller images and faster pulls, and the dependency layer stays cached when only the code changes
- [ ] It makes the image run faster
- [ ] It hides the user from `docker inspect`
> **Answer:** Layer discipline matters on every laptop and CI runner. Code is copied last so changing it does not invalidate the expensive dependency layer.

### Q5. Why are the pipeline containers run with a read-only file system and as user 10001?
- [ ] Docker requires it
- [x] Least privilege: a compromised or buggy container cannot modify its own code or write outside the output volume, and does not run as root
- [ ] It makes the analysis faster
- [ ] The CSVs are read-only
> **Answer:** An analysis container needs to read the export and write one folder. Everything else is denied by default.

### Q6. What does pushing the tag `v1.0.0` trigger?
- [ ] Nothing: tags are only labels
- [ ] A new golden file
- [x] The deploy workflow: the four images are pushed to GHCR with the version, and the optional Render deploy runs if configured
- [ ] A merge of `solution` into `main`
> **Answer:** `on: push: tags: ["v*.*.*"]` ties releases to tags, so the image version always matches the code that produced it.

## 7. What you learned
- Presenting an analysis as a product: dashboard, memo and recommendation on one screen.
- A safe AI feature: aggregates in, guardrails out, a visible deterministic fallback.
- Small, non-root, read-only Docker images with few layers, and Compose for pipelines, parity and the app.
- Smoke tests that include the failure of an external dependency.
- Releasing with a tag: CHANGELOG, runbook, images on GHCR, optional free deployment.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-7 phase-6-end      # = v1.0.0
git diff phase-5-end phase-6-end --stat
```

steps.title: Phase 7 · Data refresh, monitoring and a post-mortem
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
The memo went out; the Head of Product approved the experiment and asked for the numbers again on
the **August export (2026-08)**. You run the same pipeline on the new folder and it stops:
`data contract violated: sessions.channel.accepted (878 rows)`. That is the contract doing its job.
Behind it are three real-world changes: marketing launched a **referral** programme, orders now carry
a **payment method**, and app release **8.14** silently lost about 70% of mobile checkout events
for one week. In analytics, the dangerous failures are the silent ones. This phase adds a versioned
contract, data-quality **monitoring** over time, an incident **post-mortem**, and release **v1.1.0**,
without breaking anyone who reads v1.0 answers.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Diagnose a failing pipeline from its exit code and the failing check, and decide whether the data or the contract is wrong.
- Evolve the data contract with a version (1.0.0 → 1.1.0), keep the old version, and keep the answers schema backward compatible.
- Add monitoring: freshness, weekly metrics against their median, anomalies; report them without stopping the run.
- Exclude a week of broken tracking explicitly, with a post-mortem, and quantify what it changes.
- Prove backward compatibility: v1.1 reproduces the v1.0 golden file on 2026-06, and the v1.0 dashboard reads v1.1 answers.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 7.1 · Run v1.0 on the new export
```bash
git switch -c my-phase-7 phase-6-end
ls data/raw/2026-08 && cat data/README.md | head -40      # the new data dictionary
cd tracks/<yours> && make run DATA=../../data/raw/2026-08; echo "exit $?"
```
Exit code 3 (contract violated) and the check id `sessions.channel.accepted` with 878 rows. Query the
rows (`SELECT channel, count(*) …`): they are all `referral`, a new, legitimate channel. The data is
right; the contract is out of date. Write that down before touching anything.

### Step 7.2 · Version the contract (1.1.0)
1. Copy `contract/data-contract.yaml` to `contract/history/data-contract-1.0.0.yaml` (never edited again).
2. In the live contract: `version: "1.1.0"`, add `referral` to the accepted channels, and add a
   `monitoring` section (`max_relative_deviation: 0.30`, `max_days_behind: 2`).
3. Read `contract/questions.md` §6 and the `(v1.1)` notes in the cleaning steps; read
   `spec/adr/0006-versioned-contract-and-monitoring.md`.
4. A pipeline must still accept a 1.0 contract: missing `monitoring` means the defaults, missing
   `exclude_weeks` means no exclusion. Add a unit test for that.

<!-- track:python -->
`funnellens/monitoring.py`: `full_weeks()`, `monitoring()` and `payment_methods()`; `clean.py` drops
excluded weeks after the other session rules and counts `sessions_excluded_week`.
<!-- /track -->
<!-- track:sql -->
`sql/06_monitoring.sql` and `sql/07_payment_methods.sql`; the runner passes `exclude_weeks` and the
monitoring thresholds as parameters (`cfg_exclude_weeks`), so the SQL stays declarative.
<!-- /track -->
<!-- track:r -->
`R/monitoring.R` (`monday_of()`, `full_weeks()`, `monitoring()`, `payment_methods()`); `clean.R`
records the exclusion in `ISSUE_ORDER` so the issue counts stay in contract order.
<!-- /track -->

### Step 7.3 · Monitoring finds what the checks missed
Run v1.1 on 2026-08 **without** excluding any week first (`exclude_weeks: []`). Every check passes
except one warning: `orders.without_checkout.ratio` (113 orders, 3.3%). Then look at
`answers.monitoring.anomalies`:

| week | metric | value | median | deviation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-W31 | mobile_checkout_given_cart | 0.107 | 0.534 | −80% |

Mobile users did not stop paying (orders exist without a checkout event: that is the warning).
The **tracking** broke. The release notes confirm it: app 8.14 shipped on Monday of W31 and the
hotfix 8.14.1 the next Monday. Weekly monitoring turned a vague warning into a dated cause.

### Step 7.4 · Exclude the week, and write the post-mortem
Add `exclude_weeks: ["2026-W31"]` with a comment that names the incident. Re-run: 1,218 sessions
excluded, no warning, no anomaly. Then write `docs/postmortem-2026-W31.md` in the blameless format
(summary, impact, timeline, root cause, detection, what went well, what went badly, action items
with owners). Quantify the impact on the decision: with W31 left in, the payment-step uplift moves by
about ₹0.2 lakh/month and the recommendation does not change, but the weekly chart shows a false
collapse that a reader could take for a real drop. With W31 excluded, the CMH odds ratio is 0.725
and the uplift ₹14.3 lakh/month: still `run_targeted_experiment`.

### Step 7.5 · Payment methods
The new `payment_method` column answers a question the experiment design needs: which methods mobile
users choose (UPI 1,252, card 413, COD 267, net banking 140 orders). The experiment should test the
redesigned payment step on UPI first. `payment_methods` is `null` on exports without the column.

### Step 7.6 · Golden file, backward compatibility, parity
```bash
make coverage                     # unit + data tests, incl. the golden subset on 2026-08 (repo: tracks/<yours>)
make run DATA=../../data/raw/2026-08
python3 ../../scripts/parity.py ../../contract/golden/answers-2026-08.json out/answers.json      # IDENTICAL
make run DATA=../../data/raw/2026-06 OUT=/tmp/fl-2026-06
python3 ../../scripts/parity.py --backcompat ../../contract/golden/answers-2026-06.json /tmp/fl-2026-06/answers.json
```
The v1.0 dashboard must still render v1.1 answers (the schema only adds fields): try it with the
`phase-6-end` image. The v1.1 dashboard adds a **Monitoring** tab and two facts for the narrator.

> **A parity story worth telling.** When the three tracks were first compared on 2026-08, the SQL track
> counted `sessions_unknown_channel` after excluding the week and Python before it. Both followed the
> spec, because the spec did not say. The fix was a sentence in `questions.md` (count after step 9),
> not code in one track. Ambiguity in a spec shows up as a parity failure: that is what parity is for.

### Step 7.7 · Release v1.1.0
Update the runbook (a "data refresh" section: run, read the exit code, read the monitoring tab,
decide: data issue, contract change or incident), the CHANGELOG (`## [1.1.0]`: Added, Changed,
Fixed), the default export (`EXPORT=2026-08` in `.env.example` and the Makefiles), then tag `v1.1.0`.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Diagnose the failing refresh
```text
My analysis pipeline stopped with "data contract violated: sessions.channel.accepted (878 rows)" on a
new monthly export. Here is the contract section and a sample of the failing rows: <paste>. List the
possible explanations (data error, upstream change, contract out of date), what query would tell them
apart, and what I should change in each case. Do not propose relaxing the check without evidence.
```
**Verify the output by:** running the query it suggests yourself and checking the answer against the
data dictionary of the new export. Reject any fix that makes the check pass by deleting it or by
mapping `referral` to `unknown`.

### Prompt 2: Design the monitoring rule
```text
I want to flag weeks whose data looks broken: weekly sessions and the mobile checkout-given-cart rate
compared with their median over the full weeks of the month, flagged above a 30% relative deviation.
Here are the weekly values: <paste>. What are the weaknesses of this rule (partial weeks, small
counts, seasonality, a real change versus broken tracking), and what would a stronger rule look like?
```
**Verify the output by:** computing the deviations by hand for two weeks and comparing with
`answers.monitoring`, and checking that partial weeks are excluded as the spec says. Record one
weakness in the post-mortem's "what went badly" or action items.

### Prompt 3: Review my post-mortem
```text
Review this post-mortem for a data incident: <paste docs/postmortem-2026-W31.md>. Check that it is
blameless, that the timeline has times and sources, that the impact on the decision is quantified,
and that each action item is specific, owned and verifiable. List what is missing; do not rewrite it.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking each of its claims against the incident data (dates, counts,
deviations) and the CHANGELOG; add only the items you agree with, and note in `AI_LOG.md` which ones
you rejected and why.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] `contract/history/data-contract-1.0.0.yaml` and the live contract 1.1.0 (referral, exclude_weeks, monitoring).
- [ ] Monitoring and payment methods implemented and tested in your track; a 1.0 contract still accepted.
- [ ] `golden/answers-2026-08.json`, backward compatibility on 2026-06, parity `IDENTICAL`.
- [ ] `docs/postmortem-2026-W31.md`, ADR-0006, the runbook update.
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` 1.1.0 and the tag `v1.1.0`.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. The v1.0 pipeline exits 3 on the August export. What is the right first move?
- [ ] Remove the failing check
- [ ] Map unknown channels to `unknown`
- [x] Look at the failing rows and find out whether the data or the contract is wrong
- [ ] Re-run until it passes
> **Answer:** The contract stopped the run on purpose. Here the rows are a legitimate new channel, so the contract changes, with a new version and a note.

### Q2. Why is the old contract kept in `contract/history/`?
- [ ] Git cannot show old versions
- [x] Old answers files cite `contract_version 1.0.0`; keeping it lets anyone reproduce them and lets the pipelines test that a 1.0 contract still works
- [ ] The dashboard reads it
- [ ] It is required by YAML
> **Answer:** A versioned contract is part of the reproducibility of every past result.

### Q3. All checks pass except a 3.3% warning. Why was W31 still a problem?
- [ ] It was not: warnings can be ignored
- [x] Row-level checks look at the month as a whole; only the weekly view showed that mobile checkout-given-cart collapsed by 80% in one week
- [ ] W31 had too many sessions
- [ ] The warning threshold was wrong
> **Answer:** Checks validate rows; monitoring validates behaviour over time. You need both.

### Q4. Why exclude W31 instead of "fixing" its missing checkout events?
- [ ] Excluding is faster
- [x] The lost events cannot be recovered; imputing them would invent data, while excluding a documented week is transparent and its effect can be measured
- [ ] The contract forbids changes to events
- [ ] W31 is a holiday
> **Answer:** Exclusion with a post-mortem and a quantified impact is honest; imputation of a broken funnel step would bias the very metric under study.

### Q5. What does "backward compatible" mean for answers schema 1.1?
- [ ] v1.1 answers are identical to v1.0 answers
- [x] It only adds fields: a v1.0 reader still works, and on the old export every v1.0 field keeps its value
- [ ] It removes unused fields
- [ ] It can only be read by the v1.1 dashboard
> **Answer:** `--backcompat` compares every v1.0 field on 2026-06, and the v1.0 dashboard renders v1.1 answers.

### Q6. Parity failed on a count during the refresh. What did that reveal?
- [ ] A bug in DuckDB
- [ ] That one track should be deleted
- [x] An ambiguity in the spec: two correct readings gave two numbers, so the spec was clarified
- [ ] That parity checks are too strict
> **Answer:** Independent implementations are an excellent spec review. The fix was one sentence in `questions.md`.

## 7. What you learned
- A failing contract check is information: diagnose before you change anything.
- Versioned contracts and additive schemas keep old results reproducible and old readers working.
- Weekly monitoring against a median finds silent tracking failures that row checks miss.
- Blameless post-mortems with a quantified impact on the decision.
- Independent implementations (parity) expose ambiguities in a spec.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-8 phase-7-end      # = v1.1.0
git diff phase-6-end phase-7-end --stat
```

steps.title: Phase 8 · Retrospective and portfolio
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
Hiring managers for analyst roles see hundreds of Titanic notebooks. What they rarely see is an
analysis that states a decision, survives messy data, quantifies uncertainty, reproduces in CI and
in Docker, and was re-run on new data with an incident handled properly. You have all of that, but
only if a reader can find it in a minute. This phase turns the repository into a portfolio piece:
a README case study, an honest retrospective, and a walkthrough you can give in an interview.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Present the case study as problem → approach → result → evidence, with numbers and links.
- Write a retrospective that separates what worked, what did not, and what you would change.
- Explain your statistical choices (CMH, Welch, intervals) and their limits in plain language.
- Describe your use of AI precisely: where it helped, where you rejected its output, and how you verified.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 8.1 · Collect your evidence
Make a list with links: the green CI run on `v1.1.0`, the parity job, the coverage numbers, the
report (`tracks/<yours>/out/…`, rendered as a CI artifact), the dashboard screenshot, the memo, the
post-mortem, the ADRs, and two or three `AI_LOG.md` entries where you corrected the AI.

### Step 8.2 · README case study
Insert a **Case study** section under the badges of `README.md` (see the `phase-8-end` README):
1. **The question**: mobile is 69% of sessions but 61% of revenue; rebuild the mobile checkout?
2. **The answer**: run a targeted experiment on the mobile payment step first.
3. **The evidence**: the payment-step gap within channels (CMH odds ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.62-0.81),
   no difference in order value (Welch p 0.53), the aggregate cart gap explained by the channel mix
   (Simpson's paradox), an estimated ₹16 lakh/month below the ₹25 lakh rebuild threshold.
4. **How it is built**: three tracks with identical answers, a data contract, CI, Docker, a guarded AI narrator.
5. **What happened next**: the August refresh, the W31 tracking incident, v1.1.0.
6. **Limits**: observational data, one month, a sampled export; what the experiment must measure.

<!-- track:python -->
Link the executed notebook (`notebooks/analysis.ipynb`): GitHub renders it, including the charts.
<!-- /track -->
<!-- track:sql -->
Link `out/report.md` from a CI artifact or commit a copy under `docs/`: every view as a table is
easy to read on GitHub.
<!-- /track -->
<!-- track:r -->
Publish the knitted `analysis.html` (a CI artifact, or GitHub Pages) and link it: R Markdown output
is the most readable report of the three tracks.
<!-- /track -->

### Step 8.3 · Retrospective (`docs/retrospective.md`)
Use the template on `phase-8-end`: what went well, what went badly, what surprised you, what you would
do next, and the AI section (where it saved time, where it was wrong, how you caught it). Use evidence:
"the parity check caught a spec ambiguity in v1.1" beats "testing was useful".

### Step 8.4 · Practise the walkthrough
Five minutes, out loud: the question, the data problems (name two), the method and why (CMH rather
than a pooled z-test), the result with its interval, the decision rule, the incident, what you would
do next. Then answer the three questions in the quiz below without notes.

### Step 8.5 · Share it
Pin the repository on your GitHub profile, add the dashboard screenshot to the README, and post a
short write-up (what you found, one chart, one lesson) where your network is. Tag the final commit
`phase-8-end` if you follow the tags.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Draft the case study from evidence
```text
Here are my project facts: <paste the answers.json summary, the CI run link, the parity output, the
post-mortem summary and three AI_LOG entries>. Draft a README "Case study" section of at most 250
words: question, answer, evidence (with the intervals), how it is built, what happened next, limits.
Use only the numbers I gave you, keep their precision, and make no causal claims.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking every number against `answers.json` or the post-mortem, deleting
any adjective you cannot back with evidence, and making sure the limits section survives the edit.

### Prompt 2: Mock analyst interview
```text
Act as a hiring manager for a product analyst role. Read my case study: <paste>. Ask me eight
questions, one at a time, mixing statistics (why CMH, what the interval means, multiple testing),
data quality (what you dropped and why), business (why the threshold), and judgement (what would
change your recommendation). After each answer, tell me what a strong answer would add.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking its "strong answer" notes against `contract/questions.md`, the ADRs
and a statistics reference before you adopt them: an interviewer persona can be confidently wrong too.

### Prompt 3: Retrospective review
```text
Here is my project retrospective: <paste docs/retrospective.md>. Point out vague items without
evidence, missing failures, and action items that are not specific. Do not add achievements.
```
**Verify the output by:** keeping only changes you can support with a link (commit, run, log entry).

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] README case study with numbers, intervals and links.
- [ ] `docs/retrospective.md` with evidence and an honest AI section.
- [ ] A five-minute walkthrough you have practised once out loud.
- [ ] The repository pinned, a screenshot, and (optionally) a public write-up.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Which README claim is strongest?
- [ ] "Advanced statistical analysis of e-commerce data"
- [ ] "Used AI to find insights"
- [x] "Within channels, mobile completes the payment step less often (CMH OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.62-0.81); the estimated uplift (₹16 lakh/month) is below the rebuild threshold, so I recommended an experiment"
- [ ] "Cleaned a large dataset"
> **Answer:** A specific, bounded, verifiable result tied to a decision. The others are unfalsifiable.

### Q2. An interviewer asks "So the mobile checkout causes lost revenue?" Best answer?
- [ ] "Yes, the p-value proves it"
- [x] "The data is observational: the gap holds within channels, which rules out the channel mix, but other differences between mobile and desktop users could explain it; that is why I recommended an experiment"
- [ ] "Probably, the effect is large"
- [ ] "Correlation is never useful"
> **Answer:** Show what the analysis does establish, what it cannot, and what would.

### Q3. Why did you use the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test instead of a pooled two-proportion z-test?
- [ ] It is more modern
- [ ] It needs less data
- [x] Device and channel are related; CMH compares mobile and desktop within each channel, so the channel mix cannot create or hide the gap
- [ ] The z-test cannot handle percentages
> **Answer:** The aggregate cart gap reversed within channels (Simpson's paradox), which is exactly the confounding CMH controls for.

### Q4. What belongs in "What I'd do next"?
- [ ] "Use deep learning"
- [x] "Design the experiment: payment-step variant on mobile UPI users, primary metric payment completion, sample size for a 5-point lift, guardrail on order value"
- [ ] "Make the dashboard prettier"
- [ ] Nothing: the project is finished
> **Answer:** A concrete next step that follows from the limits of the current analysis.

### Q5. How should you describe AI use in your portfolio?
- [ ] Hide it
- [ ] "AI did most of the analysis"
- [x] Specifically: what you used it for, examples where you rejected or corrected its output, and how every number was verified (tests, parity, golden files)
- [ ] Only mention it if asked
> **Answer:** Honest, specific AI use with verification is a strength; the AI_LOG is your evidence.

### Q6. Which retrospective item is most useful?
- [ ] "Testing was good"
- [ ] "Statistics are hard"
- [x] "Parity between three implementations exposed an ambiguity in how unknown channels were counted after a week exclusion; next time I would write a worked example for every counting rule"
- [ ] "I should have started earlier"
> **Answer:** Evidence, a cause and a specific change of practice.

## 7. What you learned
- Presenting an analysis as a portfolio case study: question, answer, evidence, limits.
- Retrospectives with evidence and specific changes.
- Explaining statistical choices and their limits to non-specialists and interviewers.
- Describing AI assistance honestly, with your verification process.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-final phase-8-end
git diff phase-7-end phase-8-end --stat
```
